The Moon has a familiar face.
Why do we always see the same side of th: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
One orbit. One rotation. One surprisingl: One orbit. One rotation. One surprisingly elegant answer.
Look up at the Moon tonight. Its familia: Look up at the Moon tonight. Its familiar pattern of dark plains always faces roughly the same way.
The Moon turns once on its axis in about: The Moon turns once on its axis in about 27.3 days. It also takes about 27.3 days to orbit Earth.
This matching rhythm is called synchrono: This matching rhythm is called synchronous rotation. As the Moon moves around Earth, the same side keeps facing us.
A gentle apparent wobble, called librati: A gentle apparent wobble, called libration, lets us see about 59% of the lunar surface over time.
Does the Moon rotate on its axis?: Does the Moon rotate on its axis?
Exactly. Its rotation and orbit take the: Exactly. Its rotation and orbit take the same amount of time, so the same side faces Earth.
An ocean of blue. But why?: An ocean of blue. But why?
What gives the ocean its blue color?: What gives the ocean its blue color?
There is more to it than a reflection of: There is more to it than a reflection of the sky.
A glass of water looks clear. Yet a deep: A glass of water looks clear. Yet a deep ocean often looks blue. The depth makes a difference.
Light is a mix of colors: Light is a mix of colors
Sunlight contains many wavelengths. Wate: Sunlight contains many wavelengths. Water absorbs the red part of the spectrum more strongly than the blue.
As light travels through deep water, mor: As light travels through deep water, more of the red light is absorbed. The light that returns to our eyes is often blue.
Plankton, sediment, depth and reflected: Plankton, sediment, depth and reflected sky can all change the color. That is why coastal water can look green or turquoise.
Which part of visible light does water a: Which part of visible light does water absorb more strongly?
Yes. Red light is absorbed more strongly: Yes. Red light is absorbed more strongly, helping explain the blue appearance of deep, clear water.

Meet the quiet chemistry happening all a: Meet the quiet chemistry happening all around you.
Inside a leaf, tiny structures called ch: Inside a leaf, tiny structures called chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, a pigment that captures light energy.
Roots supply water. Small pores in the l: Roots supply water. Small pores in the leaves let in carbon dioxide from the air.
Photosynthesis uses light energy to help: Photosynthesis uses light energy to help turn water and carbon dioxide into sugars that support the plant.
Oxygen is released along the way. The gr: Oxygen is released along the way. The green world around us is doing chemistry with sunlight, every day.
